report:
Conclusion: the claim is false. Garlic is a healthy food and can show antimicrobial activity in lab settings, but that does not translate into curing COVID-19 in people. WHO’s myth-busters state there was no evidence from the COVID-19 outbreak that eating garlic protected people, despite general antimicrobial properties (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). The “Australian garlic cures COVID” story was rated false because the research was in test tubes, not humans (https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/garlic-covid-cure-claim-crushed-by-experts/). AFP likewise found health professionals had said since early 2020 there was no evidence onion/ginger/garlic/lemon tonics are effective COVID-19 treatments (https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19). The specific viral recipe—boil chopped garlic, eat it and drink the water—was directly debunked (https://factcheck.newsmobile.in/can-a-bowl-of-freshly-boiled-garlic-water-cure-novel-coronavirus-heres-the-truth/).

Evidence for the belief rests on anecdotes and extrapolation from in-vitro antiviral effects, not randomized trials or clinical outcomes. Risk: using garlic water instead of testing, vaccination, or timely care can delay effective treatment. For symptoms or high-risk illness, follow clinician/public-health guidance.
